messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: City Council Member
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 54

**Vignette: Claire, Age 39**

Claire grew up in a terraced house in a mid-sized English city, the eldest of three children. From the time she was about six years old, she learned to read the atmosphere of her home the way other children read the weather — watching for the particular set of her father's jaw when he came through the door, listening for the pitch of her mother's voice, calculating how much time she had to get her younger siblings upstairs before things turned dangerous. Violence was not constant in her childhood home, but it was always possible, and that possibility shaped everything. She remembers pressing herself against the wall at the top of the stairs, her brother and sister tucked behind her, listening to her mother cry out below. She did not go down. She has never entirely forgiven herself for that.

Claire is now a city council member, a role she pursued, she says, because she wanted to make places safer for people who couldn't protect themselves. She is articulate, driven, and widely respected. She chairs a subcommittee on housing and community safety. Colleagues describe her as unflappable. She finds this description quietly unbearable.

She has been married to her husband, Daniel, for eleven years. He is gentle and patient, and she knows this about him the way she knows facts about a foreign country she has never fully allowed herself to visit. When he raises his voice — even in laughter, even to call the dog — something in her body responds before her mind can catch up. Her chest tightens. Her vision narrows. She is thirty-nine years old and she is also six, at the top of the stairs, waiting.

The hypervigilance has been with her so long she mistook it for competence. She is always the first to notice tension in a room. She reads faces obsessively during council meetings, tracking microexpressions the way a forecaster tracks pressure systems. She rarely sleeps past four in the morning. She lies in the dark and listens to the house, cataloguing sounds, reassuring herself of their ordinary meaning.

The nightmares began again last spring, after a constituent came to her surgery appointment with bruising along her jaw and a story Claire recognized in her bones. She sat with the woman for nearly two hours, helped her contact a support service, did everything correctly. That night she dreamed she was a child again, frozen on the stairs, and her mother's voice was the constituent's voice, and she still did not go down. She woke gasping at 3 a.m. and sat on the edge of the bath for an hour so as not to disturb Daniel.

Since then the dreams have come several times a week. She avoids the constituency office on the evenings she knows certain cases will be discussed. She has started taking a longer route to work to avoid passing a house on Marlowe Street where, six months ago, police were called to a domestic incident. She drove past it once and had to pull over, hands shaking on the wheel, the past and present briefly indistinguishable.

She does not talk about any of this with Daniel. She worries that naming it will make her seem fragile, and fragility, in her experience, invites harm. She tells him she is tired from work, which is also true. She loves him and keeps him at a careful distance and understands, intellectually, that these two things are related.

What brings her to therapy is not the nightmares or the sleeplessness or the drive past Marlowe Street. What brings her is a moment in a council chamber three weeks ago when a male colleague raised his voice during a budget dispute and Claire, for one terrible second, could not remember where she was. She sat very still, her hands flat on the table, and waited for it to pass. It passed. But she is tired of waiting for things to pass. She has been waiting since she was six years old, and she is beginning to wonder what it might feel like to finally come down the stairs.
